name: Resveratrol topical
lead: Resveratrol (3,5,4'-trihydroxy-trans-stilbene) is a plant polyphenol found in grape skins, berries, peanuts and cocoa, and in Japanese knotweed root used for most supplements.[1] Applied to the skin, it appears in serums, creams and brightening products where it is marketed as an antioxidant aimed at fine lines, uneven tone and general signs of photoaging.[1][5]

Much of the published topical work concerns delivery: resveratrol dissolves poorly in water and is sensitive to light, so researchers have tested nanocarriers, emulsions and gels to increase how much stays in the skin.[2][3][4] On the human side, an 8-week randomized placebo-controlled trial in healthy women over 40 reported reduced visible signs of skin aging with trans-resveratrol, and small registered trials of resveratrol-containing products exist.[5][6][7] Wikipedia's general resveratrol article states that no significant evidence of an effect on aging skin has been shown.[1]

paras: Topical resveratrol is used in products aimed at wrinkles, uneven pigmentation and dullness, typically in leave-on serums and creams, often alongside other antioxidants such as vitamins C and E or ferulic acid.[1][5] Proponents describe it as a way to add antioxidant protection to the skin surface, so that the skin looks firmer and more even over time.
Formulators favour the skin route partly because taken by mouth the compound is rapidly metabolised, which makes delivery to skin tissue from supplements inefficient (see Pharmacology).
It has also been tested in formulations for psoriasis, burn wounds and skin cancer in laboratory and animal settings.[8][9][4]

Resveratrol is a stilbenoid polyphenol found in grape skins, blueberries, raspberries, mulberries and peanuts, and red wine is a commonly cited dietary source, with an average of about 1.9 mg per litre of trans-resveratrol reported for red wine; white wine contains much less because it is fermented without the skins.[1] Most supplement and cosmetic-grade material in the United States is extracted from the root of Japanese knotweed.[1]
Its low solubility in water and tendency to degrade are recurring themes in formulation work, which is why serums often pair it with stabilising carriers or other antioxidants.[1][2]

Resveratrol was first reported in 1939 by the Japanese chemist Michio Takaoka, who isolated it from white hellebore (Veratrum album), and it was isolated from Japanese knotweed roots in 1963.[1] Interest grew with red wine and longevity research; in 2004 Harvard professor David Sinclair co-founded Sirtris Pharmaceuticals, whose first product was a resveratrol formulation, and GlaxoSmithKline bought the company in 2008 for about 720 million dollars before closing it in 2013.[1] Cosmetic companies adopted resveratrol during the same period as a skin-care antioxidant.

Resveratrol became widely known beyond skin care through longevity research. Sirtris Pharmaceuticals, co-founded in 2004 by David Sinclair, began with a resveratrol formulation; GlaxoSmithKline acquired the company in 2008 for $720 million and closed it in 2013 without a successful drug.[1] Wikipedia's overview of human trials reports no high-quality evidence that oral resveratrol extends lifespan or has a substantial effect on any human disease, with mixed results for blood pressure, glucose and cognition.[1] Skin products draw on the compound's popular reputation as a polyphenol from red wine and grapes.

Oral bioavailability is described as about 0.5 percent because of extensive liver and intestinal glucuronidation and sulfation, and the parent compound has a half-life of roughly 8 to 14 minutes, while its conjugates last more than nine hours.[1] This is one reason research has turned to the skin as a route and to carriers that raise skin retention.

Chitosan and gum Arabic Pickering emulsions increased cutaneous retention and lowered permeation in porcine skin ex vivo and improved photostability.[2] Nanostructured emulsions raised transdermal deposition in another study, and nanocarriers were reported to enhance transdermal bioavailability.[3] A vesicular elastic nanocarrier gel was developed and tested in an imiquimod-induced psoriasis model, and nanofibers loaded with resveratrol nanocrystals have been explored for skin cancer therapy.[4][9]

In laboratory assays resveratrol behaves as an antioxidant and produces effects in many different test systems. Wikipedia notes that it is classed as a pan-assay interference compound, meaning it tends to register in many assays, and that it may act partly through direct effects on cell membranes.[1] Proposed molecular targets include NQO2, GSTP1, estrogen receptor beta, CBR1 and integrin alpha-V beta-3, and it is considered unclear which of these accounts for observed effects.[1] It is also described as a phytoestrogen.[1]

Cosmetic marketing usually frames it as a surface antioxidant that helps the skin cope with environmental stress. The studies cited in this article examine that idea through delivery into the skin and through short skin-appearance trials rather than through a settled mechanism.

An 8-week randomized placebo-controlled trial published in Frontiers in Aging in 2025 tested trans-resveratrol in healthy women over 40 and reported reductions in visible signs of skin aging.[5] A registered early phase 1 trial of topical extract and other nutraceuticals for wrinkles and pigmented spots has unknown status (n=25).[6] A phase 4 trial of a resveratrol-containing product (Replenix) on functional and emotional benefits in acne was terminated (n=43).[7]

Animal work includes a rat study in which 5 percent resveratrol ointment was compared with silver sulphadiazine and untreated controls on full-thickness burns.[8] Human evidence on appearance is limited to the small studies above.

Adverse effects in the general resveratrol literature are mainly gastrointestinal (nausea, stomach pain, diarrhea) and are reported with long-term oral intake of around 1,000 mg per day or more; few human safety studies exist and all are small.[1] The GHS hazard label for the pure compound lists eye irritation.[1] Topical adverse effects are not described in the general article.

For oral use, Wikipedia reports that adverse effects such as nausea, stomach pain, flatulence and diarrhea occur mainly with long-term intake of 1,000 mg per day or more.[1] These oral findings do not describe topical products, and topical tolerability is assessed separately in the trials above.

card.summary: An antioxidant stilbene sold in anti-aging serums, with one small recent trial and mostly delivery-formulation research behind it.
card.note: Poorly stable and poorly absorbed; human skin evidence is a few small studies.

quick.overview:
Topical resveratrol is a plant antioxidant used in anti-aging and brightening skincare. Research so far has centered on how to get it into skin and keep it stable.

One 8-week randomized trial in women over 40 reported fewer visible signs of aging, but the human evidence base is small.
quick.mechanism: It is marketed as an antioxidant. Studies on delivery show nanocarriers and emulsions can raise how much stays in the skin in laboratory models.
quick.risks: The sources describe no topical adverse-effect data; reported side effects of resveratrol are mainly gastrointestinal with high oral intake. It is light sensitive and degrades easily.

chain: Marketed to counter oxidative stress from sun and pollution
angle.text: People use resveratrol serums and creams as an antioxidant step aimed at fine lines and uneven tone. One 8-week trial in women over 40 reported fewer visible signs of aging.
